357:                                    Integrating experiments and simulations
358:                                    While the MD simulations are overall in good agreement with the SAXS and NMR NOE data, there
359:                                    remain discrepancies that could contain information about the conformational ensemble of DH5-
360:                                    DMPC in solution. We therefore used a previously described Bayesian/Maximum Entropy (BME)
361:                                    approach (Hummer and Köfinger, 2015; Różycki et al., 2011; Bottaro et al., 2018; Cesari et al.,
362:                                    2016; Bottaro et al., 2020) to integrate the MD simulations with the SAXS and NMR data. Briefly,
363:                                    the BME method refines the simulation against measured experimental averages by balancing (1)
364:                                    minimizing the discrepancy between the simulation and the observed experimental averages and (2)
365:                                    ensuring as little perturbation of the original simulation as possible thereby limiting chances of over-
366:                                    fitting. The outcome is a conformational ensemble that is more likely to represent DH5-DMPC in
367:                                    solution. In practice, this is achieved by changing the weight of each configuration in the ensemble
368:                                    obtained from the MD simulations, and we therefore call this a ‘reweighted ensemble’ (Bottaro and
369:                                    Lindorff-Larsen, 2018; Bottaro et al., 2020). The amount of reweighting can be quantified by an
370:                                    entropy change (Srel ) that reports on how much the weights had to be changed to fit the data
371:                                    (Bottaro et al., 2018) (see Materials and methods). Alternatively, the value feff ¼ expðSrel Þ reports
372:                                    on the effective ensemble size, that is what fraction of the original frames that were used to derive
373:                                    the final ensemble (Orioli et al., 2020). We note that we reweight each individual conformation in
374:                                    the ensemble, and thus that the clustering is only used for presenting the results. In this way we
375:                                    avoid uncertainties that come from difficulties in clustering heterogeneous ensembles.
376:                                        We used both the SAXS and NOE data individually, as well as combined, to understand the
377:                                    effects of each source of data on the reweighted conformational ensemble (Table 2). We note that
378:                                    when a specific type of data is used to generate the ensemble, the resulting c2 simply reports on
379:                                    how well the simulation has been fitted to the data; because of the maximum-entropy regularization
380:                                    to avoid overfitting, we do not fit the data as accurately as possible. The two types of experimental
381:                                    data complement each other in structural information content. Specifically, the SAXS data report on
382:                                    the overall size and shape, and is sensitive to both protein and lipids through atom-atom pair distri-
383:                                    butions in a range starting from » 10 Å, whereas the NOEs contain local, specific atom-atom distan-
384:                                    ces from the protein belts of the DH5 but not any direct information about the lipids.
385:                                        We find that refining against a single of the two data types only improves the MD trajectory with
386:                                    respect to the structural properties it is sensitive to, highlighting the orthogonal information in the
387:                                    two sources of information. In addition, we performed reweighting with the methyl NOEs and the
388:                                    amide NOEs separately (Figure 3—figure supplement 4). The already low discrepancy of the amide
389:                                    NOEs barely improves while the discrepancies of both methyl NOEs and SAXS are unaffected by
390:                                    integration with amide NOEs alone, implying that the structural information content contained in the
391:                                    amide NOEs (mostly secondary structure) is already correctly captured by the force field and starting
392:                                    structure. Because the NOE and SAXS experiments provide independent information we refined the
393:                                    ensemble against both sets of data (Figure 3). We find that we can fit both sources of data at rea-
394:                                    sonable accuracy without dramatic changes of the weights away from the Boltzmann distribution of
395:                                    the force field (feff ¼ 18%).
396:                                        Finally, we used the PRE and EPR data to validate the refined ensemble. In general we find com-
397:                                    parable and overall good agreement between the original NMR/EPR structure and our MD refined
